During the Budget debate I called the attention of the Acting Minister of Finance to ia very serious incident which took place before the Supreme Court a few days ago, and which I think might well occupy the attention of the House for a few moments. As we are all aware, the Government some years ago decided to construct certain works at the estuary of the river St. Charles in the province of Quebec. The other evening when his Estimates were before the House; the Minister of Public Works (Mr. iCarvell) stated he would not continue the construction of these works. When speaking on the Budget, I drew attention to the enormous and indeed shameful waste of money that had been perpetrated in expropriating land on the shores of the river St. Charles, at or near the point where the works contracted for are being erected by the Public Works Department. As a result of the determination of the Government to dam the river St. Charles, expropriations became necessary and the property of one of the riparian owners by the name of Belanger was expropriated. The Crown' initiated proceedings, and one of the judges of the Exchequer Court was dispatched to Quebec in order to hear the evidence and arrive at a proper valuation of the land to be expropriated. At the expropriation proceedings
the Crown was represented by Mr. Bernier,
K.C., of Levis, and Mr. Belanger was represented by his counsel. Many witnesses, so-called experts, were heard and the record of the proceedings, which I have here, . is more voluminous than the Hansard of this session. Mr. Belanger filed before the Exchequer Court his petition, in which he claimed the land to be expropriated was worth the sum of $800,000. Several claimants nearby have had their lands expropriated at fantastic prices, but as these cases were settled out of court the public does not know what the awards were. But the case of Belanger, fortunately for the public and for the taxpayers of Canada, has gained some noteriety by reason of the fact that an appeal has been lodged in the *Supreme 'Court of Canada. After a number of expert witnesses had been heard. Mr. Justice Audette gave the reasons for his judgment, in which he says:
The lands in question were acquired by the suppliant for the sum of $18,165.32, and were practically yielding no revenue, save the renting of one house on lot 513, and pasture on lot 560. These lots lie In the estuary of the River St. Charles, and are nothing but a stretch of muddy soil upon which in the case of lot 560 some marine grass grows, upon which cattle may feed; but the land' is entirely covered by water at high tide, and the lot has been practically idle and no use has been made of it for years and years. Wharves may be built upon the same, as wharves may be built in fields, tout it has no access to deep water, except to the height of the water brought in toy the tide. Lot No. 513 is impracticable for building purposes. It is a beach lot. Retaining walls and fillings would have to be resorted to. Some of the witnesses contend that lot 56'0 might be used for a railway yard. Is it, indeed, conceivable that a railway could afford to spend1 thousands and thousands of dollars in building wharves for a railway yard, when other property is available inland? Some of the witnesses were candid enough to say they thought the property had very little value, but it might have value for public purposes and assessed it on that basis. In other words, that the property was of very little value to the owner, but might toe! of some good value to a party expropriating for public purposes or for a scheme like the .present works. However, it is now settled law that in assessing compensation for property taken under compulsory powers, it is not proper to consider as part of the market value to the -owner, such value as the land taken may have to the party expropriating when viewed as an integral part of the proposed work or undertaking. But the proper basis for compensation is the amount for which such land could have been sold, had the present scheme carried on by the Crown not been in evidence, tout with the possibility that the 'Crown or some company or person might obtain those powers and carry on their scheme. And, in the present Instance, who, outside of the Crown, should undertake such colossal works?

I will come to that in a moment. Mr. Justice Audette concludes:
To this sum of $215,925.19 will be added the usual 10 per cent for compulsory taking, the land having obviously been taken against the Will of the owner, making in all the sum of $287,517.61.
I wonder if it was really taken against the will of the owner.

It is clear from the reasons for the judgment that the whole of the evidence to protect the Crown was not adduced in this case, and I should like to have from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) some information as to the instructions given for the conduct of this

case. I am informed that this property was acquired some years ago toy Mr. 'Belanger and another gentleman by the name of Delisle. Delisle was diving with his wife under t'he regime of communaute de hiens, and on her death had to file at the registry office in Quebec in connection witn the payment of taxes on the estate of his wife the valuation, he placed on his own property, and I am informed that the Crown could have secured that very important and very valuable document when the case was heard before Mr. Justice Audette, hut this document was not filed. It would then have been proved beyond the shadow of a doubt that the owners themselves placed a very, very low value on the property. At all events, Mr. Justice Audette, with much reluctance, to use his own words, awarded the sum of $215,000, in round figures, and added to that 10 per cent for compulsory expropriation, which made the total $237,517.61. The 'Crown appealed from that judgment. The Crown was represented there again by Mr. Bernier, K.C. Much to the surprise and astonishment of the Bench, when Mr. Bernier appeared before the Supreme Court a few weeks ago, he accepted on behalf of the Crown the award of $215,925.10, and only contested the remaining ten per cent for compulsory expropriation.
IMr. CARVELL: According to the factum, did the Crown protest against the award or only against the ten per cent?
Only against the ten per cent.
That is what counsel did. But what was in the factum?

I have the factum. filed by the Crown, andi here are the conclusions :
We therefore pray that the said sum of $21,592.51, representing ten per cent on the amount of $215,925.10 fixed as the value of the lands expropriated, be struck out from the sum of $237,517.61, awarded by the Exchequer Court.
So the Crown only contested the ten per cent. Otherwise it accepted the judgment.

As this has something to do with the department over which I preside, I am naturally interested in getting the facts. My hon. friend has produced the factum filed by counsel representing the Crown. I have some knowledge of the procedure in these cases, and I know there would be a notice of appeal given by the Crown preceding the factum.

Is there any protest in that by the Crown against the award of $215,000?
(Mr. LEMIEUX: I have here the statement of the Crown through the attorneys, Bernier, Bernier & deBilly, and I have just read the conclusion of their petition. My hon. friend knows from his long practice at the Bar that a factum is filed weeks and months before the hearing of a case. The judges of the Supreme Court read this factum, and the factum of the respondent, and when Mr. Bernier appeared before the court and stated that his only appeal was against the ten per cent for compulsory expropriation, the judges expressed their surprise because they had read very closely the reasons for judgment of Mr. Justice Audette, and the proceedings were stopped by the court, and if my information is correct-the Minister of Justice is better informed on this point than I am-the Supreme Court sought new instructions from the Department of Justice.
This is clearly a case where the Government should investigate and where the Department of Justice should he exceedingly careful. There seems to have been gross neglect in connection with this important litigation. A sum of $237,000 deserves some attention and consideration in view of the reasons for the judgment given by the Exchequer Court. What has taken place 1 do not know, but it seems to me that the Department of Justice should, in view of the incident of the Supreme Court, and in view of the reasons for judgment given by Mr. Justice Audette, revise these proceedings and give new instructions in order to prevent a scandalous claim from being paid. Here, you have the whole case in a nutshell. These beach lots cost the owner $18,000. They did not yield enough to pay the tax bills, the claim made was for $800,000 and because of the laches of the Crown, because of the absence of witnesses and experts on behalf of the Crown, the judge was compelled to award with reluctance, as he says in his judgment, a sum of $215,000 plus 10 per cent. The Crown, represented by its agent before the courts, and knowing more than anybody else the reasons given by the judge, yet accepts the judgment as to the amount of $215,000 and only contests for the smaller bit, a sum of $15,000. There is something strange, something mysterious, and I hope the minister will explain to the satisfaction of the House what happened in this case and what action he has taken since to prevent that scandalous amount from being taken away from the exchequer of the Dominion at the present time.
Would the hon. gentleman tell me whether or not either or both of these lots, or any portion of them, is now occupied by works constructed by the Department of Public Works on the St. Charles river?

I am informed that the barrage, the damming, of the river is above those lots. I could quite understand the Crown expropriating lots above the dam but I am informed-and I speak subject to correction-that these lots are below the barrage and are therefore not seriously affected by the proposed works. I say the "proposed" works. My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell) declared the other day that he would stop these works. I do not know what his intentions are but this is an exorbitant amount that is being claimed under the present circumstances.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. member (Mr. Lemieux) in his statement of the case, seems to have attached particular importance to empnasiz-ing the part which the Crown took in the matter. There is not any doubt that the Crown was represented by counsel. The facts in regard to the direct action of the Crown are that the instructions were of the clearest possible kind that an appeal should be made from the entire award, and the appeal which was lodged under the immediate direction of the Deputy Minister of Justice, as the departmental records will certainly show, was an appeal from the entire award. But the hon. gentleman says that it was greatly to the surprise of the court when counsel charged with the case made the declaration. I may say it was as great a surprise to the Department of Justice, as great a surprise to the deputy minister who had given the instructions, as it seems to have been to the court. These instructions, I am informed by the deputy minister, were clear and distinct that the entire award was to be appealed from. What misapprehension the counsel seems to have laboured under it is quite impossible for me to explain. Certainly his action as .1 have said, was not in accordance with the instructions that he had received. The gentleman who 'had been retained and who was representing the Crown is, I do not think it will be disputed, a gentleman of repute and standing in his profession. I cannot undertake to explain how he came to misapprehend his instructions and to take the line of action that he did. I suppose it is to be assumed that for some reason

lie was of the opinion, differing from the opinion expressed by the hon. member that the evidence for whose production he was responsible supported the judgment. If he entertained that view it was not shared by the department, and his instructions were such as I have stated. When the incident occurred, and when it was brought to the attention of the department, steps were at once taken to see that this erroneous representation was corrected and that the matter was put in such shape as to ensure that the case of the Crown attacking the award itself should be put in the most perfect manner possible before the court. Further, instructions, as I am informed, were given that, if upon a careful examination of the entire evidence, it should be deemed necessary, steps should be taken looking to a reference back to the court if there should be any deficiency in the evidence which it would be possible to supply. While the fact is undoubted that the learned counsel who was retained to carry on the case did take the view which the hon. member has -stated, it is equally true that in taking that view he- was not -acting in -accordance with the instructions winch were given to him, and that tnat view was not shared by the Department of Justice. That the -gentleman in question should have been retained I have not heard suggested as ground for complaint. I understand that Mr. Bernier -has b^en the batonnier of the bar of his district, and enjoys a good reputation as a member of the profession. It is an incident most reg-rettable that he -should have so misunderstood his instructions, -but that is something, I suppose, that might happen with respect to the legal representative of any client. It might happen that the instructions of any client might be misunderstood or not fully grasped, and that is the regrettable thing that appears to have happened to the Government in this particular case. But the hon. gentleman and the House may rest assured that the appeal itself, as I have pointed out-which is a direct action on the part of the Crown taken under the direction of the department itself-was an appeal against the entire award, and, as- I have said before, I am informed by the deputy minister that the instructions were precise that the entire award was to be appealed against. When it was brought to our knowledge that those instructions were not being acted upon, -steps were taken at once such as I have already indicated, steps to see that the contentions of the Crown, as against the [IMr. Doherty.]
amount of the award itself, should be fully put before the court, and looking also- if that were deemed necessary or advantageous-to securing a sending of the reference back to the court below for the purpose of taking further evidence in the event of it being found both desirable and possible.
I do not know that I can add anything further. Those are the facts. Upon that set of facts I do not think that the department or the deputy minister, who is directly responsible insofar as the direction of these cases come -under his hands, can be open to legitimate reproach. The most that can be said-and it is a most regrettable thing to have happened-is that the counsel that the Crown had retained to conduct the case-because it is quite clear it is not possible for the officers of the department to conduct all of the litigation which goes on on behalf of the Crown- apparently misconceived, or misunderstood the directions which he had received, or formed a judgment of the merits of the case, which was not in accord with the appreciation of the -department.

There is no
d-ouibt whatever, from the explanation given by the Minister of Justice, that n-o (blame can -attach to the Crown, which was simply unfortunate in its selection of the counsel who conducted the -case. I am glad to hear from my hon. friend that ithe- instructions given to the new counsel are to hav^ the case referred back to the Court of Appeal for the production of other evidence.
iMt. THOMAS VIEN (Lotbiniere): Were any explanations asked for, or received, from the counsel as to his conduct in the case?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not in a
position to say. I certainly have not taken the matter up, nor am I in a position to state at the present -moment what communications have passed between the deputy minister and the counsel. There is room in this case- for demanding an explanation, and that explanation- will certainly be asked for.
To whom has- the case been entrusted for future action?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand that Mr. -Chrysler has been retained, and that the deputy -minister is personally interesting himself in the matter.

As this matter relates to the Department of Public Works,
I do not think I ought to allow the opportunity to pass without making a statement which possibly may have something to do

As to that phase of the case, 1 have nothing further to say, because it does not rest with my department, tout with the Department of Justice. Knowing, however, Mr. Justice Audette as well as I do, and realizing how carefully he weighs the evidence -and I speak now from personal experience and knowledge-I cannot read the judgment which he has .given in this case without coming to the conclusion that he had a very strong opinion that something had been' withheld from the court, and he was awarding more for the land than he was justly entitled to. From my standpoint, as Minister o'f Public Works, that is a very serious part of the case. I know generally where these works are, although I have never examined them carefully. Because if we have not got the lands, from the description I have received of theim I do not think we need them, and I know well enough how to get rid of them.

I do not wish to occupy the time of the House 'any longer than merely to say ta few words further. I am satisfied with the explanation given by the Minister of Justice that he will see to it that decisive and direct instructions shall be given to Mr. Chrysler to look after this case. speechtext:

Post Office Department-salaries, $943,870 ; contingencies, $125,000.

It is rather strange, living as we do under British institutions, that for the last three years we should have been deprived of a responsible head of the Post Office Department. But what is most extraordinary, indeed, is that the Postmaster General, having been defeated at the last election, should still be the incumbent, although he is not attending to the duties of his department. I know of only one similar instance in 'Canadian history At the very inception of responsible government, when the Governor was attempting to bar the way to its attainment, two gentlemen were sworn in as ministers in the Draper-Viger administration, under Sir Charles Metcalfe, if I mistake not. They went before the people and were defeated, yet they were retained in the Government. After some time, however, there w.as a reaction in public opinion, the Draper-Viger administration had to resign, the Lafon-taine-Baldwin ministry succeeded, and Canada has since had an uninterrupted succession of cabinets possessing the confidence of the people. Since this case of Mr. Viger and Mr. Morrison, no gentleman sworn in as cabinet minister and afterwards overwhelmingly defeated by the electors has been maintained in oflice against the popular will. Aside from the constitutional revolution which such a precedent creates, what are its consequences? During last session and since the beginning of this session we have not once been able to discuss seriously the administration of the Post Office Department-and heaven knows that it needs investigation. The expenditure of the Post Office Department has more than doubled since 1911. If a responsible head of that department was in the House we could discuss .These matters and certainly impugn its administration. What reason can the leader of the House give for such a nefarious precedent? Are there not gentlemen behind the Government who are able to occupy the position of Postmaster General? Is it fair for the Government to place the administration of the Post Office Department in the hands of a gentleman who does not belong to this House and is not appointed to the other? Hon. Mr. Blondin has not been elected by the people, and for him to draw his salary as minister of the Crown is rather surprising. I repeat that this is a dangerous precedent; it is on a par with the kind of government we have had since the beginning of the war. I need not say that my heart is in this war, but I regret that I ever gave my assent to the War Measures Act as it has been framed and applied. The country is being shorn of its liberties; Parliament of its constitutional rights. It is being shorn of its privileges and of its ancient usages. The constitution has become a by-word in Canada. The country is governed by Order in Council passed before, during and after sessions of Parliament, under the shallow pretense of winning the war. Mr. Chairman, we are fighting in Europe for the very liberties which are being denied to the Canadian people. I hope that the leader of the Government will give this Committee and the country the reasons why the Post Office Department has no responsible head, and whether this scandal is to continue during this fiscal year.

I do not know that in the Committee of the House is the proper place to make statements with reference to the matter brought up by my hon. friend. I do not think things are quite as blue as he has tried to make them appear. These are extraordinary times. The late Minister of the Post Office-
Is it the late minister?

-and the present Minister of the Post Office, not now representing a constituency, is doing more than speaking in favour of the war. He has actually put himself to the test of the war, and is to-day at the front doing his quota in sustaining the war effort. I think that it to he taken into account. I grant you that constitutionally the assent of the people to the possession of a constituency is the normal ground for the continuance of a departmental head in office, but there has not been a lack of instances, in our own or other countries constitutionally governed, where that general principle has been passed by under temporary or extraordinary circumstances. This certainly

is no ordinary circumstance; it is an extraordinary one, and I do not think that for a short period the people of this country will find any great fault with the action of the Government in reference to Mr. Blondin under the circumstances to which his absence from this country is. due. iHe is doing where he is a service to the country equally as great as he could do here in Canada in administering a department of Government. The Post Office Department has not lacked for direction and Government during his absence. It has been under the care of a judicious and careful administrator. My hon. friend makes no point when he cites the fact that the expenses of the Post Office Department have increased during the last two or three years, and attempts to draw from that the conclusion that it is because of the absence of the departmental head. There are other reasons which account for the increase in the expenses of the Poet Office Department and which will be amply explained by the administrator of that office when, in .a few minutes, we come to his Estimates.
In reference to the more general subject as to Government of the country by Orders in Council under the War Measures Act, we are under experiences which are not different from those of all warring countries, and although we may talk academically with reference to loss of rights and privileges, there is not a single man of us who enjoys one iota less of his freedom, of his liberty, of his well-being, on account of the peculiar methods which do obtain in governments of countries in any period of great war and the stress which arises therefrom. If my hon. friend had been a member of a government during this war, he would have resorted to the very same measures. It is impossible not to do so. Let us take the case of the United States. The people of that country are, to a large extent, suffering a curtailment of the privileges of its legislative 'bodies such as in normal times they never would submit to for a single moment. They submit to it because the exigencies of war call for it, and it is impossible to have direct and strong action such as is necessary in war times, if you have to observe all the methods which obtain in normal times when everything has to pass through legislative channels. I do not think we are really very much hurt in the matter. As to the imputation of my hon. friend that he and the country have suffered from the Government which has been in power during the last three or four or five years, I am quite sure that the
['Sir George Foster.]
country had just as good an idea as my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) of what the Government had done and what they expected the new Government to do, when in 1917, they reposed an unbounded confidence in the present Government, although they may not have had as much practical acquaintance with governmental and administrative methods. When the war is all over, my hon. friend will not be the last to give his meed of commendation and praise for the way in which, and the methods by which, the present Government, and, I may say too, the past Government, have conducted the affairs of Canada in their objective of pursuing the war to a victorious conclusion.

Without questioning what the leader of the House (Sir George Foster) has said, or what the leader of the Opposition. (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has said,

may I point this out? This country is about to take over a great railway. We are to have a national railway, and with that rail-*vyay goes a national telegraph system. Therefore, at a period like this, a Postmaster General ought to 'be in office so. as to administer that national telegraph system, if the telegraphs are, as I imagine they are, to go under the administration of the Post Office Department. I should like to see not only a strong Minister of Railways, but a strong and active Postmaster General to administer the national telegraph system. .

Mr. Chairman, I concur in the
statements made a moment ago in reference to this matter by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux). Under the circumstances, Mr. Blondin's absence is not only detrimental to the proper management of the Post Office Department, but it gives rise to a state of things which is contrary to public interest. As a matter of fact, the maintenance of Mr. Blondin at the head of that department, under the circumstances, is in defiance of public opinion, more especially of that of the people of the province which defeated the ex-minister at the last election, in two of the most important electoral districts of Quebec. French Canadians-and they constitute a most important section of the people of this country-are not represented in this Cabinet. We are not anxious to be represented in this Administration as now made up, and the remarks I have just made should not be construed as implying such a desire on our part. 'But let me say this: As long as the French Canadians have no representative in this Cabinet, at least let us dispense with that camouflage which is resorted to at present and in justification of which arguments quite as worthless are put forward.
Under the British system, it is contrary to every principle of constitutional government that a member of that Cabinet should be maintained in office and should continue to advise the Crown after ceasing to be a member either of the Senate or of the House of Commons. It makes no difference whether we are at war or not; I say to the Government that they violate every principle of responsible Government when they maintain in office a man who was defeated at the polls. As stated by my hon. friend the member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux), it seems as though, under the present regime, Parliament no longer exercises any rights in this country. Public affairs are settled by Orders in Council. We are left in ignorance of what is going on, the most important matters are disposed of without Parliament having any opportunity to interfere in any way. As an illustration, Mr. Chairman, take the question of prohibition; it is a most important matter. I, for one, would likely favour some measure of prohibition, especially during the war; but I am earnestly opposed to the settlement of the question through the Government, without Parliament being consulted, notwithstanding the fact that the hon. the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) is a member of the Administration.
A few days ago, a member of this House was elected by Order in Council. If the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Thompson) sits in Parliament to-day, he owes it to the fact that, on February 26, the Governor General in Council abusing the powers conferred on them by the War Measures Act, suspended the working of the electoral law in this country, so that a partisan might secure a seat in this House.
We had been told that this Union Government, as the offspring of the Parliament which was to be elected on December 17, would exert some influence over the future of this country, because political partisanship would disappear and we were, at last, to see independence prevail in Parliament. We have had instances of such independence here within the last two or three days, members who, though they had been elected under the Union flag, under the flag of independence, cast their votes in direct opposition to the views they had expressed, because the Prime Minister had said: " If you vote in favour of abolishing titles in Canada, or else if you wish to prevent me, as Prime Minister of this country, from giving titles to my friends, although I am in favour of winning the war and have been elected to win it, I shall give up the job, and shall tender my resignation to His Excellency." Mr. Chairman, that such conditions cannot be tolerated much longer is quite apparent, because they are objected to by all right thinking people, and I would ask the Government, as also the Acting Postmaster General to give us some assurance to the effect that the Post Office Department will be put under the management of one who is the choice of the majority of the electors in some constituency of the Dominion.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment
speechtext: The policy that has been followed heretofore with regard to tubercular cases is to utilize the existing tubercular institutions. In many cases these institutions have been enlarged, and arrangements have been made with some of the institutions for the payment at so much per bed, the institutions taking complete charge of the cases. The large number of tubercular cases coming up for treatment have made it necessary for many of the tubercular institutions of the country to be enlarged; in many cases the accommodation has been doubled, but in each case a separate arrangement was made between the Military Hospitals Commission and the owners of the institution, or the provincial government operating the institution, as the case may he, on whatever might be mutually considered fair terms. With regard to insane cases, a uniform method of treatment is followed in all the provinces. At the conference of provincial premiers held in Ottawa, I think in November last, an arrangement was arrived at whereby all the incurably insane were to be cared for in provincial institutions, and the provincial governments were paid by the Military Hospitals' Commission a fixed sum per head per year.

Might I suggest that there may be great difficulty on account of these institutions being at the present time very much overcrowded? We cannot get half the accommodation we require in the province of Ontario for the treatment of civilian tubercular and insane cases. It strikes me the soldier end of this matter - hould be handled by the commission direct.

Special allowance to the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Canada, to oover travelling and other expenses in connection with his services while acting as Deputy to His Excellency the Governor General, $5,000.

I hope I shall not be misunderstood in raising objection to this item. I do not want to be understood as being parsimonious in regard to the salaries that should be paid to the judges in this country. I should not object if the salary of the Chief Justice of the Dominion of Canada was doubled; I would not put my judgment of the worth of his services against the judgment of hon. gentlemen in this House who are of the legal fraternity and therefore better able to judge the value of those services than I am. But I do not like this roundabout way of adding to a man's salary, whether it be the Chief Justice of Canada or anybody else, and it does seem to me this is a roundabout way of adding to his salary. If the judgment of this House 'was that his salary should be $15,000 or $20,000, I should not object, but I say it is ridiculous, illogical, and unreasonable on the face of it, to say that $5,000 is necessary to eover travelling and other expenses in connection with the services of the Chief Justice while acting as Deputy to His Excellency the Governor General. The Chief Justice of Canada, I understand, comes down here once in a while to sign certain documents and act as the Deputy of the Governor General when His Excellency is away. If he is to be paid for that service, well and good, but to say that $5,000 is a fair remuneration for the work done is not in my opinion reasonable. Why does the item appear in that way? It must .look to the general public as unreasonable, and that being so, it does not reflect credit on this House or upon hon. gentlemen. I agree that the position of our judges calls for such remuneration as will enable them to maintain the dignity of their position; I am quite in accord with that idea. But let us look at this thing reasonably and face the facts fair and square. Let us vote the Chief Justice of Canada a salary that is fair and reasonable according to his position, instead of voting him a salary which in the judgment of the members of this House is only half what he should get, and then making up the deficiency in some- roundabout way.
I would call my hon. friend's attention to the fact that

it is not exact to say that this is an addition to the salary of the Chief Justice of Canada. The history of this vote is this. At all times since we have had a Governor of Canada, there has always been an Administrator of Canada, or a substitute for the Governor, so that if the Governor was called away or was incapacitated for one reason or another from discharging the functions of his office, the executive head should not be wanting in Canada; there would always be some one to represent Royal authority. In the olden days the officer who discharged these functions when the Governor General was away was called the Administrator, since known as the Deputy to the Governor General. In the olden days the Administrator was the General Commander of the Forces who at that time was residing in Halifax. We had in those days garrisons at Halifax, Montreal, Kingston and Toronto, but the garrisons were moved from one place to another until at last we had only one garrison, and that was stationed at Halifax. The Commander of the Forces lived in Halifax and as it was inconvenient for him to come to Ottawa in some short absence of the Governor, . it was thought advisable, and this dates back I think to the days of Sir John Macdonaldi's Government, to have the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Canada made the Administrator or Deputy Governor, and the salary was attached to the office at that time, if I remember correctly; I think I am right in that, but I speak subject to correction. It was thought advisable afterwards to give the salary as Administrator to the officer who happened to be the Chief Justice of Canada, That is the reason for this vote. Whether it is too high or not is another matter. I simply wanted to call the attention of my hon. friend to the fact that this is not an addition to the salary of the Chief Justice. We must have an officer for this purpose, and if it is not the Chief'Justice it must be somebody else. 'I simply rose to correct the observation of my hon. friend, and to say that this sum is not an addition to the salary of the Chief Justice, because sometimes the duties of the Deputy Governor have been performed by a puisne judge of the court who has received the remuneration. This remuneration is attached to an office which I think ought to be remunerated.

Permit me, Mr. Chairman, to express my thanks to the rigid hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) for the ex-

planation which he has so fully and kindly given. I am very glad, indeed, to get it, because this is the first time I have heard a full explanation of the matter. Perhaps that is my fault. I repeat, I have no desire whatever to he unjust or unfair to any man in this country, the Chief Justice or any one else, and 1 am very glad, indeed, to get this explanation, which I think was due to the members of this House, and which possibly it is not against the interests of the Chief Justice himself for the public generally to know.

This special
allowance to the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court to pay his travelling and other expenses while attending the sittings of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council goes back to the days when Sir Oliver Mowat was Minister of Justice. At that time the then Chief Justice, Sir Henry Strong, went to England to sit as a member of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council under an Act which had been passed by the Imperial Parliament inviting judges of colonial courts to sit with the members of the Judicial Committee. Their services were required especially fox colonial cases. The Government of that day, at the instance

of Sir Oliver Mowat, placed an. item in the Estimates of $2,500 to cover the travelling expenses of the Chief Justice.' I do not remember the exact wording of the item, but it was to pay the travelling expenses of the Chief Justice while attending the sittings of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, or some such wording as that. This item goes back to 1897. It was for travelling expenses. It appeared in the Estimates in that form until 1915 or 1916, when the item was changed from "travelling expenses" to "special allowance." Under this the Chief Justice received his travelling expenses to attend the court, when, in fact, he had not attended the court. Why this change was made from "travelling expenses" to "special .allowance" I do not know. That was not in my time. It was in the time of the present Government. What the explanation of it is I do not know.
The late Government.
The present Government.
The late Government.	[DOT]

No, not the late Government; the present Government. It may have a new complexion now but that is only a veneer; it is always the same old Government. They changed the words "travelling expenses" to "special allowance" and the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) made the statement lately that it was paid monthly. It so happened that in one or two years the Chief Justice was not called upon to attend the sitting of the Judicial Committee and on those years he had received the money. If the item had been left as it was before with the wording "travelling expenses" the money could only have been paid when there were travelling expenses, but it was changed to "special allowance" and there the matter stands to-day.

As I have intimated
once before in this House I often feel myself at a loss in discussing some of these questions when I have to pit my poor abilities against those of a lawyer who has had training along legal lines, knows the intricacies of the law and knowing also how to make a bad case out of a poor one.

Well, I will leave it at that, because the case, although poor before, is worse now. The wording of the item was changed from "travelling ex-

penses" under which, as the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) says the money could only be paid when he travelled, to "special allowance." What is the' significance of the word "special"? If it was a special allowance I would imagine it would be granted for a special purpose and if it was for a special purpose, what was that purpose? Unquestionably it was to pay his expenses if he went overseas to attend the Privy Council. He did not go to attend the sittings for two years but he drew the $2,500 nevertheless. One might criticise paying a man $2,500 to cover travelling expenses even if he did go over, because, if you allow for a first-class passage on one of the best boats that cross the Atlantic and grant him a liberal remuneration during the six or seven weeks that he stays in Great Britain attending the Privy Council, his expenses will come far short of half of $2,500, let alone $2,500. I would not call in question the payment of the $2,500 if he had actually gone across to attend the sittings of the Privy Council. But it does seem to me that no amount of twisting-I do not use the word in a discourteous sense-no amount of camouflage can get around the fact that $2,500 was paid for a specific purpose which purpose was not carried out and he therefore was not entitled to that $2,500. There is only one thing that a member of Parliament can do and that is to insist that that money shall be handed back to the treasury of this country. If we have not some assurance along that line, there is only one thing I can do and that is to ask that this item be struck out. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As to their nature, they are precisely the services of a member of any court. When the 'Chief Justice of Canada goes over to sit in the Privy Council, as has been pointed out, he sits as a member, hardly of a court, but as a member of the Judicial Committee, which is the ' proper designation, which advises His Majesty as to the disposition which should be made of the cases.
Does he prepare the cases?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
He sits as a judge sits, hears the cases, as one of the committee composed of a number of members. When they have heard the cases and studied the cases, they form their judgment, and he takes part in that judgment with the other members of the Judicial Committee. As I understand it, provision is made qualifying the Chief Justices, or the judges of certain courts in the Dominions, upon invitation of the Judicial Committee, to join with them in the hearing of cases. It is found, I think, particularly desirable in connection with colonial cases. Upon that invitation, when the Chief Justice acts upon and sits as a member of the Judicial tribunal, his duties as such are purely judicial, that is to say, to hear with the other members of the committee the cases and to make up his mind with the others as to 
what the proper .judgment is to be rendered.
He does not have to do with hearing the evidence in advance or anything of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, he sits like any other member of the tribunal.

I want to call attention to one other thing. In the year 1914-15 the vote was "travelling expenses of Sir Charles Fitzpatrick attending sittings of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, $2,500." This amount was paid, as Sir Charles Fitzpatrick attended sittings of the Privy Council in August, 1914. In 1915-16 the vote was "special allowance to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick to cover expenses in connection with Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, $2,500." He drew it that year. Now, I have a right to ask, inasmuch as this is a vote to cover expenses in connection with the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, what expenses were incurred to warrant the payment of that amount? The wording is being changed this year to read as follows: "Special allowance to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick to cover expenses when attending the sittings of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council." That makes it, of course, that he cannot get it unless he attends. The 6nly difference then in the wording in the two years is that the one year says "when attending." Now, if you say he is entitled to $2,500, whether he attends [DOT] or not, to cover, expenses in connection with the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, then it is up to this Government, or to those who think that the money should be voted, to show what those expenses were, or to show what trouble he was put to which would justify the paying of that amount to cover expenses. In the one case we have travelling expenses. When he travels, it is actual travelling expenses. We can understand that. In the other case, he does not travel, and gets the amount still to cover expenses. No travelling in that case: then what are the expenses? The idea unquestionably was to pay him $2,500 to cover his expenses in attending sittings over there. It is unreasonable to suppose otherwise. That being the case, when he did not attend, when he was not put to any expense for travelling, it seems to me self-evident that he has no business to draw the amount for services he did not perform.

There is no doubt about the wording of this vote. Is there

any doubt in the mind of the Committee that if we have a representative on the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, and we send him there, that we ought to pay him his travelling expenses, the expenses that he has incurred in doing that duty? The vote is so worded that it shows its intention explicitly. And I am quite willing to say that not a cent of that money will be paid unless the service is rendered. Under that, has my hon. friend from Fron-tenac any objection to the vote passing?
I will also say that I will get the information and give it to him, I hope, before this session is over, with reference to the two preceding years.

My right hon. friend (Sir George Foster) has asked me a question, and I will answer it. I am not prepared to let the vote go through. I am in the judgment of the House; I am only one. But the fact that, in my judgment, five thousand dollars of the -money of Canada has been taken out of the Treasury by a man who happens to 'be Chief Justice of the Dominion of Canada, warrants me in saying that I will not consent to the passing of another item of $2,500 to that gentleman until I know that that money will be refunded.
I think we must let this item stand until a later time, and come back to it again. When I have the information I will give it to the House, and then the House can make its own decision.

I suggest that instead of providing a specified sum for Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, we vote an amount for the duties performed and expenses incurred1. Two thousand five hundred dollars would not be too much to grant for the duties performed.

That would be a great mistake. I do not see why the Chief Justice of this Dominion should not be in the same position as that occupied by the humblest civil servant in the country so far as this matter is concerned.
