I notice that the country has lost the valuable services of the Postmaster at Toronto. The postmasterships of Toronto and Montreal are the most important in Canada; these are the largest offices, yield the largest revenue and incur the largest expenditure of any in Canada. The press of Toronto are unanimous in their desire that the late Mr. Rogers, the former postmaster in that city, be soon replaced. We have just passed a Bill which is supposed to bring about Civil Service reform. Will the leader of the House inform me, without giving names

I understand that he must be very discreet about such appointments-whether it is the intention of the Government to select by promotion from within the ranks and according to merit only, a successor to the late postmaster at Toronto?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Under the Civil Service Act all appointments are made by the Civil Service Commission, who will doubtless proceed in accordance with the provisions of that Act. I understand that the question is presently engaging their attention.

Perhaps I am too exacting, but I am not satisfied with my hon. friend's answer. Various rumours are afloat and prominent names have been published in the press in connection with the vacancy in the Toronto post office. Will the Government fill this vacancy by appointing an officer from within the ranks on the principle of promotion and according to merit?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman does not seem to -grasp what I pointed out: that the appointment is not in the hands of the Government; therefore, the Government cannot say who will be appointed. The ' Government will appoint nobody. The Civil Service Commission will make the appointment, and I have no doubt that -they will give consideration to the point raised by my hon. friend. I do not speak positively, but I think that the principle of promotion such as my hon. friend -suggests is laid down for the guidance of the Civil Service Commission.

I must express my regret at the manner in which the public business of Canada has been handled during the last two or three days. I think I am right in saying that this is the first time that we have had before us any item which permitted the discussion of post office affairs.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The post office estimates have not been up before to-day.

It is now half past eight o'clock, and I am informed that at ten o'clock His Excellency is to come down with the expectation of proroguing this Parliament. It is very desirable that we should do business expeditiously. But I want to say this: I shall not use the word " protest " because that is too strong a word, but*I believe I voice the general opinion of the House when I say that this is not a fair way to do the business of the Dominion of Canada. I realize the necessity of the Prime Minister and some of his colleagues going away, but certainly that is no reason why the whole work of Parlia-. ment should be rushed through in the way in has been done during the last two or three days. We have had 'meetings of the committees at ten o'clock in the mornings; the House has met at eleven o'clock in the morning; it has met in the afternoon; it has met in the evening, continuing till all hours of the night; and now at this stage of the session we are, for the first time, within an hour and one-half of prorogation, taking up the Estimates of one of the greatest departments of the Government and we are in a few minutes going to vote $19,000,000 for that department. I want to say, in no spirit of fault-finding, that this is not a proper way of doing business, and I do not think the Government are justified in rushing business through in this way. While it may be quite necessary to provide for the absence of the Prime Minister, he has able and competent colleagues who could take charge of matters in his absence, and we should have been able to sit here for a fe&r days longer and conduct the business of the House as it should have been conducted.

I wish to emphasize the remarks made by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens. I shall not delay the proceedings of the House, but I shall simply ^ give a few facts which will show how this whole business is badly managed.
Has it not always been the same?
No, it has not.

My hon. friend says that we are going to vote $19,000,000 without having had a single minute during a session of nearly three months to discuss the affairs of the Post Office Department. I said before dinner that the expenditure in that department had doubled since 1911.
[iMr. Fielding:.]
I have the figures under my hand. In the public accounts I find that in 1910-11 the expenditure in that department amounted to $7,954,222. In 1911-12 it jumped to $9,172,035. In 1912-13, it was $10,882,804; in 1913-14, $12,822,058; in 1914-15, $15,961,191; in 1915-16, $16,009,138, and in 1916-17, $16,300,578.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: How much has the revenue increased in that time?

I know that the special war tax has increased the revenues of that department, but putting that tax aside, as it should be, the revenues have practically remained the same while the expenditure has been more than doubled. That is a very unhealthy state of affairs. I do not wish to delay the proceedings of this House, but I shall simply enter my protest. We have had no opportunity to discuss the postal administration, and yet we are face to face "with this bald fact that, in 1910-11, the expenditure of that department was about $8,000,000, whilst for the last fiscal year it had reached the enormous figure of $16,300,000, with no more revenue than in 1911, with the exception of the war tax.
'Mr. DOHERTY: The hon. member has pointed out that, in the last seven years, there has been, as he states, no increase in the revenue, if you eliminate the special tax. I am assured by those who know the facts that in that he is quite mistaken, and he shuts his eye to the fact that there has been an immense expansion in the business to be carried on by the Post Office Department. We have nad a great extension of the rural mail route deliveries. We have had an immense increase in the parcel post business which has necessarily entailed an additional cost of the service rendered to the public. Anything so unfair as taking the bald statement that more money is being spent in the year 1918 than was spent in the year 1911, and concluding that that necessarily implies improper expenditure, I think it would be difficult to suggest. As to our having such a very short time to deal with this miatter, we have been in readiness, on different occasions, to lay these Estimates before the House, and the delays that have prevented us are not attributable to the Government. Yesterday we spent one whole day that might have been usefully employed in discussing in detail these very Estimates, in discussing a motion that prevented us from going into this matteT. On other occasions attention has been given to matters that

are certainly less important than these Estimates, but whose is the responsibility?
I do not think this is an exceptional instance which has never occurred before. I shall not dwell upon the reasons on account of which, in the judgment of those best qualified to speak for both sides of the House, it was not thought desirable that this session should be prolonged. Those reasons commended themselves to the general judgment of the House. Those reasons have brought about this situation, wh?ch I should be glad to have avoided, but the responsibility for which does not rest, at all events exclusively, upon the shoulders of this Government and this particular department.

I would like to have from the minister a statement as to the cancellation of mail contracts. There is a great deal of unrest amongst mail contractors throughout the country, many of them claiming they are losing money by carrying out their contracts. I understand that of "late some contracts have been cancelled. Will the minister state briefly on what terms a mail contractor can obtain cancellation of his contract?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
A mail contractor has no right to cancellation of his contract. He tendered for that contract in competition with others, and got it because his tender was lower than the fenders of others. But ae I mentioned some time ago, upon a resolution on this subject, taking into consideration the circumstances and conditions which justified the belief that, in many instances, it is, at all events, probable that unexpected increases in costs have so altered the situation of the contractor as to place him in a position where he is suffering substantial loss, we did adopt, ae I explained at that time, the rule that, where a man had, under totally different conditions, entered1 into a contract which, for the reasons I gave a minute ago, might be entailing serious loss to him, we would in such oases consent to cancellation of the contract and call for tenders at the present time, putting that man in a position where he would be enabled to do the work at prices -similar to those for which others would be willing to. do it, giving him his fair chance w.ith everybody else. As I explained, I could not convince myself that it was fair to those who had failed in obtaining contracts that the man who had got it because his tender was lower in the first place than the others should retain the contract at a higher price because he
was losing money. Of course, it is not really a sound business principle to consent to cancel a contract at all, and if we were standing on our rights we would not cancel them. .But I have felt, and I think the House will justify that view, that where it was perfectly clear that a man by reason of unforeseen and unusual circumstances was in a position- where he was actually doing this work for the country at a substantial loss to himself, the country should not insist on holding him to his contract.

In the old wagon
days a certain mileage rate was allowed up to a certain sum. Possibly that has all been done away with, now that tenders are called for.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The work is let by calling for tenders.
-Sir SAM HUGHES:	Under the system
carried out by the minister one man may find that- he has submitted too low a price, but he has to struggle on. Why not return to the old system and say the rate should not exceed so much per mile or per trip? Give the department a little option in the business. I do not want to take up the time of the House, but I could give half a dozen instances where men who have the mail contract are losing money. They find themselves cut out and then the man who takes their place in turn has the same experience. I think it is hardly fair to the men who are doing the contracting.

There is a great deal of distress among the men carrying the rural mail in our part of the country, and they -would like some advance. If the minister would allow the men who have the contracts a better rate I certainly think something of that kind ought to be done, because I get letters nearly every day from men who are actually losing money on- their contracts. If the minister can possibly find a way of relieving the distress of these rural mail -carriers it certainly ought to be done.

I was desirous of bringing this matter to the attention of the House-. I read with some interest the statement made by the minister some time ago respecting the possibility of cancelling these contracts. As a matter of fact, in only one of the cases that have come to my attention has the contract been cancelled, and that was the best paid one of the lot. An absolute refusal to cancel the contract was given in every other case.

The minister has stated that as a matter of right these contracts need not and should not be cancelled because these men entered into them in a perfectly open and legal way, and knew what they were doing. It is true tenders were called for, but in almost every case it has been the practice of the Government for many years past when the tender price was a little higher than they wanted to pay, to send an inspector or some one acting on his behajf around and peddle the contract between Tom, Dick and Harry, beating them down like a Jew would until they got a certain price and in most cases the price was ridiculously low. I know a case in one part of my riding where a man for many years has been carrying the mail for a dollar for a return trip of sixteen miles, and yet he has to go on in spite of the fact that the price of everything has gone up. This man has not had a new contract for years, I venture to say, but his old contract has been renewed, the department simply saying to him that he should not ask for anything more in these hard times. Rural mail delivery contracts have been let in the past on the basis of $30 per mile per year; in other words, a man who had a trip of twenty miles would receive about $2.12 or $2.15 per day and out of this magnificent sum he had to pay the expenses of keeping a horse or a team, and pay for his meals when away from home, and when you take into account the present price of hay and oats, that leaves him 62 cents a day. I was told by one official of this Government that the matter might be remedied by letting women do the driving, and letting the men go into other employment where they might earn perhaps $3 per day. I told my informant it might be quite true of the part of the country from which he came, but that it would be absolutely unfair to ask any woman in my part of the country to drive a team twenty miles a day through snow in winter and mud in summer for the magnificent sum of 62 cents a day. I would be ashamed to offer it to any woman in the province of Ontario. These men are suffering an actual hardship, and I think the members of this House have a right to demand that where these men ask for a cancellation of their contract it should be granted at once. If a man is making any money out of the contract he will not ask that it be cancelled, but will go on with it; it is only men who are losing money who will ask to be relieved from their contract.
CMr. Arthurs.!
The minister said a few moments ago that we are getting an increased revenue and doing increased work on account of the parcel post system, but what about the poor fellows who carry the parcels twenty or forty miles away from the railroad, and sometimes require two teams of horses to draw the mail in? These men are carrying the mail for the contract price in force before the war, and before the parcel post system had reached anything like the proportions it has to-day. These men are not getting one cent extra in spite of this heavy additional work.
I want to say a word on behalf oi the country postmaster. In a great many cases it is a woman who is doing this work for $50 a year. She has the trouble of looking after the post office every hour of every day, and I think something should be done for these people. No man, let alone a woman, should be asked to put himself to the inconvenience of handling the mail in one of our country post offices for the sum of $4 a month. I think something should be done for their relief now. We are told that the estimates are doubling themselves every five years, and I think some part of the increase should be given to this very deserving class of our people.

In the early days of the session a resolution dealing with this question was 'before the House, and I believe the Prime Minister asked to have the debate adjourned with a view tj resuming it later in the session after the Government had had an opportunity of considering the matter of an increase in salary to the rural mail carriers. A few days ago I asked a question in the House, and the leader of the Government informed me that an opportunity would be given when the post office estimates were up to discuss this question.
The rural mail carriers are undoubtedly rendering a splendid service to the country, a service which is invaluable under present conditions, and at this particular time, when we are taking care of practically every branch of the public service of this country except the rural mail carriers, I think some explanation is certainly due as to why some relief has not been afforded them. Two years ago when a number of these contracts were let conditions were altogether different from those of to-day. I have a case in mind which I took up with the department about six months ago, asking that the man be relieved from his contract or be given an increase. Yester-

day I had another letter from him almost begging to be relieved from his contract, as his family was sick and he had no means, and he also urged me to see that the last part of his salary was forwarded to him immediately.
fie is in a position to 'get daily wages as an ordinary labourer that would be much greater than he gets with his team and outfit while carrying His Majesty's mail. That is surely a condition of affairs which should not exist. It is deplorable. You must realize that many of the rural mail carriers are at a time of life when they are very much below their ordinary earning power. Old, and often crippled, men who are unable to engage in ordinary labour render good service as carriers of the mail. When you stop to think of the torture that these people had to endure during the past winter you must realize the very great injustice that is being done. I do not think that I am asking too much when I ask that adequate salaries be paid to these [DOT]people. I would give some official in the department, an inspector, a superintendent, the deputy minister, or some one else, the right to exercise a little discretion in the matter during the abnormal times through which we are passing. The department ought to see that a uniform remuneration is paid for this service and that nobody is carrying His Majesty's mails at a loss. If a mail carrier is performing his duty at a loss the department ought to make up the difference. In a case such as I have referred to, where a man has gone down and out in absolute poverty as a result of carrying the mail, I think some recompense should be made. It is humiliating for the people of Canada to have public service rendered when the people who are rendering that service are unable to support themselves and their families as a result of the increase not only in the cost of living but in the cost of feed for their horses. The Government increased the salaries of letter carriers, who have only themselves and their families to support, but the rural mail carrier has a double increase to attend to. H6 has not only himself and family to provide for but he has his steed. The feed for his horses has now doubled in price, its cost is four times greater than it was when he entered into the contract. I was a little surprised that some explanation has not been given in view of the request that the Prime Minister made when the hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) moved his resolution dealing with the matter. We have been looking
day after day to see if something was going to be done in this regard. It is a matter of keen disappointment to me to find that apparently no provision is going to be made to take care of the people who are performing this service.

I just want to add a few words to what has been said :n regard to file rural mail carriers and pcsl-masters. Cases similar to those which have been spoken of by my hon. fiiend (Mr Sutherland) have come to my notice in the past three or four months. When I have lirought these to the attention of the department, I have had the same answer, that these men were under contract, that they had taken the contract at a specific price and they must carry it out. In one district in my constituency two rurai mail routes became vacant. No contractor has come forward and expressed a willingness to accept the price that the department is ready to offer. In one case the department have suggested to me that if I could get some one to take a contract they would be willing to consider a compromise and make the rate a little higher. Therefore, the whole contention about mail contracts being carried out falls to the ground. If they would simply give the contract to the lowest tenderer, whether or not such a tender was higher than the limit they had fixed instead of sending some one out to try and beat the man down to the mileage basis which was arrived at a few years ago, satisfactory contracts would probably be obtained. The only fair way is to give the mail carriers an increase in proportion to the increase which every one else in the country is receiving. I desire to say a word in regard to rural postmasters. I have had this matter also up with the department. A group of members waited on the minister and I think we made it clear that on the new basis which was established in 1915 fixing the salaries of rural postmasters there was a discrimination against the man who is in a post office with a revenue of less than $10,000 a year. Under the basis in force prior to 1915 a revenue of $10,000 gave the postmaster $3,200 a year as income. Under the new regulation a postmaster in order to get $3,200 a year has had to increase his postal revenue by 23 per cent. A postmaster in an office with a revenue of $1,000, received $500 a year, but under the new regulation he has to increase the postal revenue 52 per cent in order to get the same salary that he got before. I have spent considerable time at the Post Office Department trying to get

to the bottom of this question, but I will admit that I could not convince the officers of the department that there was discrimination. I pointed out the case of a post office in my riding where the postmaster's salary had decreased in the past two years, that whereas he was getting $208 a month prior to the change in the blasis rate-out of which he had to pay his rent, light, heat and	assistant-the	remuneration
has been reduced to $159 per month or a reduction of $49 a month while the work has been very largely increased. I have in my pocket a statement from the Poet Office Department in regard to another post office in the district I represent, where the total amount that the postmaster receives for carrying the mails and keeping the post office, with an allowance of $80 per year for night duty, is $416, including rent. When a group of members had this question up with the department we were given to understand that probably some relief might be given when the Supplementary Estimates came down. But in the Supplementary Estimates I find that there is an item put in to take care of increases to thirty postmasters where the revenue is more than $10,000, and where the salary will be $3,200, but there is not one single nickel for the rural postmaster. The condition has just got down to this, that it has become almost impossible to get a man whb can be depended upon to take charge of the post office in an outlying part of the country. Certainly, I feel that the whole scheme of remuneration for the rural postmasters and rural mail carriers should be revised and that something like reasonable compensation should be given to them.

I would like to corroborate what the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) has said. In many cases the rural postmasters are not paid what they ought to be. In some cases there are well founded complaints about the management of the post office, but nothing can be done, because when you speak to the postmaster you know he is not properly paid and you cannot find fault. The remuneration of these postmasters and mail carriers is not what it ought to be. A case came up recently in Port Arthur where a man who had served faithfully for twenty-five years died and no allowance whatever was made to those who were dependent upon him. The postmaster wrote to the department about the old and faithful servant, but nothing could be done. I think the postal department should revise their salaries and allowances.

I would like to endorse what has been said in regard to the rural mail carriers and postmasters, and to apply it especially to the postmasters in the county of Carleton. I know a postmaster within seven miles of the city who is carrying the mail seven miles backwards and forwards for the sum of $300. There is no better class in the community than the country postmasters. They have to keep their offices open from six o'clock in the morning until possibly ten o'clock at night, in return for which they receive the munificent sum of about fifteen cents a day. If the Government are not generous they should at least be just, and I think it is only right that these men should be paid fair wages. Take the rural mail carriers. They drive twenty-five miles a day generally and are paid $600 a year, which hardly suffices to feed their horses. If we expect the mails to be carried in a satisfactory manner, we ought at least to pay these men a fair wage. I hope the Government will take these representations into their earnest consideration. We do not urge an extravagant stipend, but it should at least be a just one. I do not think any man who is in charge of a post office, and keeps it clean and presentable, should be paid less $100 a year, while the mail drivers should receive at least $1,000 a year.

There is in my county a grave state of affairs with regard to the rural carriers. The people there feel that the postal department is probably the best run department in the Government service because it is administered so parsimoniously. The general public think it is a wonderful department, by reason of it being the most economical branch of the public service.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is a pity the hon. member from Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) is not one of the listeners.

I will be glad to study the situation a little and find out who is the mean man at the head of the department. I cannot say that it is my hon. friend from St. Ann, because he is only the acting minister. However, I have observed this: A man having a route of twenty-five or twenty-six miles paid for on the old standard at the rate of $30 per mile per year, refused his contract lately when it expired. New tenders were called for and only one was received, which was $200 higher than the former contractor was paid. The Government would not give the contract to the tenderer. I suppose if his tender had been $200 lower he would have

got it very quickly. The department, I presume, said to the inspector: "For God's sake, see if you cannot save that $200 and get somebody to take this work."
The inspector wrote to the former contractor and he refused to continue the work. The request virtually made was: " Please keep the contract .and we will peddle around and see if we cannot get somebody to take it." That was the tenor of it, for I saw the letter. The man wrote back and said: " I will not be bothered with it." Is that a fair way to do business? If the Government are going to stand by the principle of calling for tenders they should take the offer that comes in, whether it is a httle higher or a little lower. I do not think it is dignified for the Government to attempt to beat down men who have sent in a bona fide tender according to the regulations, and failing that, attempt to get the former contractor to help them out.
While on the subject of the parsimony of the department, I do not know whether the Post Office Department is blameable for this matter or not, but I know a post office janitor who has served for thirty years at the magnificent salary of $600 per year. Although he is married and has raised a family of three children, he has not had an advance of salary in all that time. That man is there yet, but is frightened of his life of being squeezed out if his health fails him and losing that miserable pittance.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand that janitor is suffering from the parsimony of the Public Works Department.

He has charge of the public building which accommodates the Excise, Customs and Post Office Branches. But it shows the parsimony of the department that they would keep a man at a salary of $600 after thirty years 9 p.m. of faithful service. Hon. gentlemen stand up in this House and talk on behalf of the under-dog and all we get is a nod of the head from the Acting Postmaster General. He does not rise and say he is going to see that grievances like this are remedied. I think that the situation in the country to-day calls, and calls loudly, for the Government to declare that the time has come when this loyal and efficient body of officials in the country districts should get some recognition and some consideration. Large increases can be easily got for the big men, but nothing is forthcoming for the little men. There is no doubt about that. Why
is it? Hon. gentlemen sitting on the front benches do not go to the country. They do not know the country. They are ensconced in Ottawa .mingling with the high fellows, the club fellows, and the top-notch fellows. They do not know the country fellows at all. It is about time they roused themselves and shook up the service. We have got a splendid body of officials, but the officials are frightened of the ministers.

Are they?
Mr. [MORPHY:	Yes, absolutely frightened, and yet some of them are men of strong parts and large hearts, but they are so repressed by the ministers that they are in a state of perpetual fright. When it comes to Sir 'Thomas This, or Sir Thomas That, it is easy enough to get a thousand dollars, it goes through hidden in the Estimates so that you cannot find it. On behalf of the Outside Service, I want the Acting Postmaster General to give the pledge to-night that, so far as this department is concerned, he will shake things up in the interest of that deserving body of men, and the same with the rest of his colleagues, so that the country's needs will be properly taken care of and what we sometimes call the "under dogs" properly looked after. You cannot expect a man to keep a wife and family of three children on such a salary as $600:
That's a large family.

There are some men in the eastern provinces who probably have more than thirteen children:. Well, for keeping the post office, furnishing fuel and light and shovelling the snow off the paths in the winter for the convenience of the public, country postmasters get the magnificent sum of $75 a year. Morning, noon, and night, these postmasters are at the behest of the public in an official capacity, subject at any time to dismissal and the loss of that munificent stipend, if somebody happens to complain that he did not receive a letter which he should have got. Services such as these are, to. my mind, public services in the true sense of the term, and these men should not be treated in the meagre, miserable, measly way in which they are treated throughout the country. I ask the ministers to realize that the Government is not getting any credit from the people for the parsimony exercised and displayed towards what might be called the inferior service, but is nevertheless the superior service, rendered by these people in the country districts. I ask again for

the most favourable consideration for the claims of these people, and that they be given a fair show.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Before recognizing Mr. Euler, who caught my eye several momenta ago, I wish to s-ay that never in my experience have hon. gentlemen kept so well to the question before the Chair as they have during the last two hours, but I must also remind them-without in any way desiring to call them to order-that there is only one hour left in which to dispose of about one hundred items in the Estimates. I understand that His Excellency the Governor General is leaving for Toronto on the eleven o'clock train, but if hon. gentlemen think that prorogation should be delayed until to-morrow, why of course it will have to be. I understood, however, that it was the desire of every one that Parliament should be prorogued to-night, but I would be very glad to have the opinion of the committee. If it ie the unanimous consent that we adjourn until to-morrow the chair man is quite willing.
Only hon. gentlemen on the other side have spoken so far.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: At the present rate, it will be impossible to meet the wishes of the Committee.

I think, Mr. Chairman, that we will be able to get through in fair time. If we cannot do it by ten o'clock, we can by a little after ten, and if not by then, then by a little after eleven. We can get our views out, and I think we can get ready for prorogation to-night. I would not have gone so far as to have suggested it to-night, but there have been many times when we have made the same general conventions. And I have consulted also with my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

My right hon. friend (Sir George Foster) will certainly acknowledge that there has been no obstacle placed by us. We have been endeavouring to further the business. But the business of the country must be done, at all events.
Oh, yes.

I shall not keep the House more than, a few moments. I thought it was absolutely in place that at least one member on this side of the House should support what has been said by seven or eight members on the other side. I absolutely agree with the argument advanced

by those who have already spoken. I believe the people of this country will absolutely endorse anything in reason that the Government will do for the relief of these three classes in the postal service- the letter carriers, whose case, I believe, has been dealt with, I think, not .altogether too liberally; the postmasters, whose remuneration, I think, is almost a disgrace to the people of Canada; and the rural mail carriers. I agree with what has been said, and I think that the Government should deal with this,not in the spirit of getting the services of these men for as little as possible but with some idea of remunerating them according to what they deserve. I think the people of this country should support *>
them in that. I will also say that, before the House prorogues, hon. members would appreciate some sort of an expression of policy on the part of the Government with regard to this matter.

There was a certain amount of disappointment in this House at the answer the Acting PostmasteT General (Mr. Doherty) gave to the question of my hon. friend beside me (Mr. Le-mieux) as to the principle which should be adopted in filling the vacancy in the Toronto Post Office. The minister said, when asked if it would be filled by merit from gome man already in the service, that the department had nothing whatever to do with it, that the office would be filled by the Civil Service Commission. We are all aware that the Civil Service Commission has a certain amount of control, but I find that the Act says that the
Governor in Council may make such regulations as he deems necessary or convenient in carrying out the provisions of the Act. There is nothing to hinder the Governor in Council from making a regulation as to the making of appointr ments. I would like to know from the minister, in view of the fact that the Government have complete control over the commission whether the principle of promotion will be applied at Toronto or will the old patronage system be followed?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman comprehends in a manner I cannot follow the provisions of the Act that the Governor in Council may make regulations to carry out the Act, while the Act says that the Civil Service Commission shall make the appointments. I wish to bring three matters to the attention of the Acting Postmaster General: First, the postage on parcels to soldiers overseas. This is a subject

that I have had in mind ever since Y came to this House in April. During the campaign in December it was impressed on me very forcibly from many quarters that it would be desirable if the Government could see its way clear to forward free of charge parcels to the soldiers overseas. Poor women who have to work hard for their money and find it difficult to pay for the material contained in the parcels sent to their sons overseas, have to pay in addition excessive amounts by way of postage On a package of ordinary size the postage amounts to thirty-eight or forty cents, and this makes the cost of the whole parcel very high. I am sure that this suggestion will appeal to the sense of fair play of many members on the other side of the House. The next matter that I have in mind is that of postage on magazines to soldiers. In the magazines published in the United States there is a notice on the cover advising the reader that if after he finishes reading the magazine he places a one cent stamp over that notice and drops the magazine in the post office, it will be forwarded to some soldier in the army or the navy overseas. I think that this also is a matter for the serious consideration of the Post Office Department. Then, there is the suggestion that the revenue from the sale of postage stamps and inland revenue stamps be kept separate. It is impossible for the Post Office or Inland Revenue Departments to determine exactly the amount of revenue received by the respective departments in respect of these stamps if they are not kept separate. Moreover, the way they are dealt with now is not businesslike. I suggest that the ministers of these two departments take this subject into consideration. It should not be possible to use a postage stamp for inland revenue purposes, and vice versa.

Before this item is carried I wish to have a parting word with the Minister of Railways on the question of patronage on the Intercolonial railway. I have brought this matter to his attention several times, but I have not yet had a clear and distinct statement from him as to the policy of the Government in this matter. We all know that the employees of the Government railways were excluded from the Civil Service Act which has just been passed. I want to tell the minister that in Eastern Canada the patronage system still exists on the Intercolonial railway notwithstanding the fact that the Prime Minister stated some months ago that it had been abolished. It has not been abolished. When I brought this matter up a few days ago the minister said that he had had a conversation with the superintendent of the road, and that he had -told the superintendent he had a free hand with regard to the question of patronage. Now that is not sufficient to bring about the reform we desire. The general superintendent will be afraid to offend members of Parliament in that part of Canada by enforcing this reform unless he is backed up by the whole strength of the minister, and the minister so far has not taken the action that is to be desired. In Nova Scotia we have a committee which looks after securing employment for returned soldiers. The committee is very active and has done splendid work in the wliy of finding employment for the men who are coming back from the front. The secretary of the committee a

few days ago wrote a letter to the master mechanic on the eastern division of the Intercolonial railway. It had occurred to this committee that some of these soldiers might be given positions as brakemen or cleaners on the railway, and this letter I have referred to was written for the purpose of eliciting from the master mechanic a statement that he would accept applications for employment of that kind from returned soldiers. Let me read the reply to that letter:

Eastern Lines.
R. H. Martin,
Superintendent Diet. No. 4.
Stellarton, N.'S., April' 2.2, 1918. Secretary, Returned Soldiers' Employment Committee,
65 Metropole Building,
Halifax, N.S.
Dear Sir:
Your letter of the 16til instant to hand, in regard to the employment of returned soldiers.
If you have two machinists, I could place them at Sydney. In regard to wipers and cleaners employed at the roundhouses, I would refer them to Mr. A. McGregor, M.P., New Glasgow, for a recommendation, as this has always been the practice when taking on employees in the railway.
Yours truly,
W. N. Ingram, Master Mechanic.
Mr. Ingram has the duty of employing men on the eastern division of the Intercolonial, and in this letter he tells the secretary of the committee that if he wants to get a position on the road for a returned .soldier as a wiper or cleaner, which is the *meanest position on the Intercolonial, the applicant must get a recommendation from Mr. A. McGregor, M. P., for New Glasgow. Imagine, Mr. Chairman, a young soldier just back from Vimy Ridge who wants a position of this kind on the Intercolonial going to the door of one of the shops on the Intercolonial and with hat in hand asking for a jbb, being told that he must first get letter of recommendation from someone distributing patronage for the district! If this is dene in the case of returned soldhrs, what will be the chances of a young fellow who belongs to the opposite political party? What I want from the minister is a plain and clear-cut statement that he will apply the rule of no patronage on the Intercolonial railway; that he will have a notice nailed on the doors of all the shops to the effect that no recommendation will be required from any patronage committee in the case of any applicant seeking a position; that men will be given positions on

their merits, and will not be required to bring a certificate from Mr. McGregor or any body else. If the minister will make ench a statement it will be quite satisfactory. I know he does not intend that, the present conditions should prevail on the road, but the conditions I have described certainly do exist at the present time, and unless some positive action is taken by the minister they will continue to exist.

I think I stated in the House a few days ago that I had informed the general manager of the Intercolonial railway, Mr. Hayes, that in operating the road he could employ any one he saw fit without regard to the political party to which the applicant belonged. I am sorry the party mentioned in that letter should take the stand he does as far as returned soldiers are concerned. The only recommendation any returned soldier wants to get a position on the Intercolonial railway or in any department of this Government is himself. The returned soldier will be given preference over everybody else. With reference to patronage outside of returned soldiers, I gave instructions to Mr. Hayes that he was to employ people on their merits, and those instructions, I suppose, he would circulate among all the officials serving under him who had authority to employ help. I gave him instructions by letter only to-day, for I have received a copy of the letter my hon. friend has read, and I will expect those instructions to be carried out. I do not think the hon. member for New Glasgow, the hon. member for Guysborough or any other member, wants to be bothered with patronage if he can get out of it; that is the way I feel about it, and I have not been bothered with patronage either on the railway or anywhere else since Civil Service reform was brought about. Neither Mr. McGregor nor any other member has recommended me to employ any person on the Intercolonial railway.
He is certainly doing it, as this letter shows.

He is assuming that responsibility himself. I do not think I could make my position any plainer than I have done. If the instructions I have given are not carried out we shall be having another session some months hence, and hon. gentlemen can come back and make any complaints they wish.

Would it not be well to put that letter of instruction on Hansard?

Department of Mines-Contingencies-for expenses of a representation of the Dominion of Canada on the advisory body of the Imperial Mineral Resources Bureau, London, England, $2,000.

I understand that this bureau is established in accordance with a resolution adopted at the Imperial Conference of last year. I am glad the right hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) is in hisi seat and that I may have an opportunity to say what I have to say previous, to his departure for London to attend another conference with certain members of the Government. The main resolution which was adopted last year, and with which I thoroughly agree, concerning the political readjustment of the different parts of the Empire, reads as follows:
The Imperial- War Conference is of opinion that the readjustment of the constitutional relations of the component parts of the Empire is too important and Intricate a sulbject to be dealt with during the war, and that it should form the subject of a special Imperial Conference to be summoned as soon as possibles; after the cessation of hostilities. ;
But I submit that other resolutions adopted at the same conference are somewhat objectionable, though it may seem presumptuous on my part to criticise in any way the statesmen who took part in that conference. What I fear is that certain gentlemen, certain groups and certain organizations, are taking advantage of the war, and of the conditions created by the war, to try to create a situation or condition of accomplished facts in order to promote their ambitions, and that they propose a readjustment according to their own view. It is said that these commissions and bureaus are only created for the purposes of the war. That was said in answer to a question asked the other day of the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen). In this connection, I wish to read to the committee the following resolution which was

adopted at the conference last year in regard to the control of resources:
The control of natural resources available within the Empire, especially those that are of an essential character for necessary national purposes, whether in peace or in war.
In regard to this Imperial Mineral Bureau, for which we are now asked to vote a sum of money, it is said:
That it is desirable to establish in London an Imperial Mineral Resources Bureau upon which should' .be represented Great Britain, the Dominions, India, and other* parts of the Empire.
So this control of what certain gentlemen call " Imperial resources " is advocated for times of peace as well as for times of war. What about this particular Imperial Mineral Resources Bureau? This Imperial Mineral Resources Bureau has been recommended by the Imperial War Conference of last year upon a suggestion by the Dominions Royal Commission, of which the right hon. the Minister of Trade and Commence was a member. I commend to the members of the committee these words which I find in the report of the commission:
It is not difficult, however, to imagine conditions even in times of peace, in which it might become desirable to use the possession of these assets .as an instrument of commercial negotiation. The practical monopoly of potash which Germany possesses has enabled her to exert pressure on other countries in the past, and the controversy between Germany and the United States in 1911 may be mentioned as an example of the influence which the possession of a raw material monopoly gives in commercial negotiations between two Powers. The possession of assets such as the Canadian asbestos and nickle supplies could be used by the British Empire as a powerful means of economic defence.
The commission, of which the right hon. gentleman was a member, recommended that the assets of Canada should be considered as belonging to the Empire as a whole and might be used to advantage by the united governments of all parts of the Empire in the negotiation of commercial treaties with foreign countries. I do not desire that this particular vote should be considered as a ratification of the resolutions, especially of the wording of the resolutions, which were adopted at the Imperial Conference of last year. The resources of Canada are national resources and should be so considered. Nothing should be done of such a nature or character as to prejudice, or interfere in any way with, the great task which will confront the statesmen of the Empire after the conclusion of the war.
IMr. E. Lapointe.]

I had expected that the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) would before his departure for the old country give us a precis of the objects of his visit to London to attend the next Imperial Conference. He had promised to make a statement to the House but he has not made it. He had also promised to give us the names of those who were to accompany him on his visit. I wish to emphasize the remarks which have been made by my hon. friend from Kamouraska (Mr. Lapointe). I do not object to the presence of the right hon. gentleman and his colleagues at any Imperial Conference provided that at that conference nothing is decided upon without the free and unshackled consent of the people of Canada. Last year's conference was held in London and several important matters were discussed. First, the navy scheme was discussed and the Admiralty was requested to work out, immediately after the conclusion of the war, what it considered the most effective scheme for the naval defence of the Empire. I would not wish to, enter upon a naval debate this evening, but while we do not object to our statesmen discussing with the Imperial authorities the actual needs of the war, the time is not ripe when they should proceed in advance and commit the credit of Canada and of the Dominions to any future naval schemes. Other questions were decided with regard to the military situation, standardization, military training, the question of Imperial resources which has been, brought up by my hon. friend from Kamouraska, and preferential treatment, this last being a very dangerous subject to discuss at the present time, because when the war is over the policy of preferential treatment between the British Empire on the one hand and the rest of the world on the other will create a very complex situation.

High Commissioner's Office, London-To provide an additional amount tor three clerks, $300.

I desire in connection with this vote to offer a suggestion, or present a request to the Government- perhaps I should say that I am only claiming a right. I was in London last year and I happened to go to the High Commissioner's office in company 10 ip.m. with two lawyers from the city of Quebec-Mr. J. E. Chapleau, K.C., and Mr. Simon Lapointe, K.C. One of my companions was curious to learn whether he could be understood in French in the High Commissioner's office. The first official to whom he spoke only shook his head. He then went into the various rooms in the building and tried to get the information he wanted, but nowhere in the High Commissioner's office in London could the French language be understood. Now, Mr. Chairman, the French language is spoken everywhere in London. In the large stores, in all the hotels, in all the public offices, and in the railway stations, notices are posted in both languages. In all the large churches, even of the Church of	England-and	thereare very few Frenchmen who belong to that denomination-French is recognized. In St. Paul's Cathedral and the other churches you will observe notices posted in both French and English. In the city of London the French language occupies the position which it enjoys in all civilized countries and among all educated people. Sir, it is a pity, and I thought it was regrettable, that the only place where French could not be either spoken or understood was the office of the High Commissioner for Canada, a country in which the French language is official. I avail myself of this opportunity to ask that this grievance be redressed, and that at least one of the three clerks who are to 'be appointed as a result of this vote shall be a person able to understand the questions of gentlemen of French extraction who may go to London and who want to be heard and understood in their own language.	,	,

My hon. friend is a little mistaken, but it is probably the wording of the item which has led to the error. The item does not mean that there are three additional clerks to be appointed to the High Commissioner's office, as my hon. friend will see when he notes that only $300 is being voted. What this means is that a statutory increase is asked for three clerks. However, that does not take away from the other portion of my hon. friend's remarks, and I shall have very great pleasure in giving the substance and the very words of his statement here to-night to the Prime Minister, under whom the High Commissioner's office is placed, and who will take the matter into consideration. I do not think that what my hon. friend has said is unreasonable.

Mr. iCAHILL:	Judging by this item
there seems to be quite a flock of lame ducks seeking shelter under the protecting wings of the Minister of Railways and Canals. And before he gets too far into the railway game in this country, into the business of acquiring all the railways in sight, he and the Government should take into their very	serious	consideration
the question of the counties which are paying bonuses to railways. The county of Pontiac, which I have the honour to represent, voted a bonus of $200,000 a few years ago to get a railroad. Of that they still have to pay $100,000. They will also have to assume their proportion of the cost of the purchase of these and other railroads; they have to stand the burden of the increased freight rates and passenger fares as well. They understood they were to be benefited by this railway when, they agreed to pay this bonus, but they have no railroad communication whatever, yet they are in a position of paying a bonus, and having to pay ferry charges eveTy time they go across the lake at Pembroke, representing an increased expenditure there of five or six thousand dollars a year to get their produce to market. While the minister is

spending money for railways in lavish amounts, I think something should be done to relieve these people of that bonus. I think other counties than Pontiac have probably paid bonuses to have railroads built. If it is the policy of the Dominion of Canada to take over these railroads, they will, I hope, not demand the payment of at least that proportion of the bonus not yet paid.

The matter referred to by the hon. member is of course a very large question, and it is the first time I have had any suggestion of this kind. I should be glad if he would put in writing to me the suggestion he has just made in order that I may give it consideration during the recess. It is too large a question to discuss here at this late hour. With respect to the several small lines in the; province of New Brunswick, covered by this item, they have been operating for years at a loss, and it is really now impossible for them to operate on account of the loss they are making. We are now taking them over, and not at a price that any one would feel is exorbitant For instance, in the case of the Elgin and Havelock railway, they have agreed to sell their lines for $30,000. The rails alone on that line, if we were to sell them for scrap, are worth about $80,000.

May I ask my hon.
friend who are the directors of that railway, or, at least, who is the president?

I could not say. There is a Mr. Pearson in Halifax, connected with it. All of these railways we are getting at about one-third the value of the rails. I have a word to say about the last two. For the Kent Northern, I have put in an amount of $60,000. They have not agreed to accept that amount. Neither have the Caraquet and Gulf Shore railway agreed- to accept the amount of $200,000. To those two lines we have made these offers, which are on about the same basis as the others mentioned before. If they do net accept, we will not pay any higher price, and these amounts will not be paid. But I am placing them in the Estimates to give them the opportunity, and to allow us to take over the lines, and thus close out the branch lines which are so unsatisfactory in the province of New Brunswick.

Out of deference to the wishes of hon. gentlemen to wind up the business of the session and get home, I do not at this stage intend to enter the protest against these purchases, which it


was my original intention to do. However,
I desire my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals-who refers to a matter relating to the county represented by my hon. friend from Pontiac, . involving, I think $100,000, as so large that he has not time to deal with it, tout who is asking us to vote $518,000 as a comparatively small sum to these other railways!-to- submit to the House at the opening of the next session the full correspondence relating to the purchases of these roads, giving all details as to the ownership and directorates in each case.

I have explained my position with regard to the Caraquet and Gulf Shore Railway, and I do not intend to rehearse the argument I put before the minister at that time. I suggested at the time to the minister that, although I did not think the proposed amount of $200,000 would be accepted, he might put it in the Estimates. He refused at the time to put it in. subsubtopic: GENERAL, THE HOUSE OF COMMONS AND THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Then I shall read the documents. The following is the communication to the Governor General:
His Excellency,
The Duke of Devonshire,
Governor General of Canada,
Ottawa, Can.
Tour Excellency:-
The undersigned, in exercising the immemorial privilege of British subjects, are confident that Your Excellency will honour the ancient practice of the highest authority in the realm of hearing sympathetically the representations of the citizens upon matters affecting the good government of Canada.
We are encouraged to transmit to you certain information by the knowledge that those who have preceded you as a representative of the Crown in the working of responsible Government in Canada, have -been swift to regard any endeavours of departure from the constitutional usages by which the freedom of Parliament and of the individual citizen has been established.
Since Your Excellency's arrival among us. we have had every reason to he assured that Your Excellency is imbued with the conciliatory far-seeing and statesmanlike spirit which animated Lord Elgin, to whom Canada and the Empire will ever be indebted for a wise and courageous guidance within the powers confided to him.
We believe, therefore, that you will welcome this expression of our trust during the period of unprecedented difficulty through which the Dominion of Canada is passing.
It is in harmony with Lord Elgin's reply to an address from the County of Glengarry, dealing with the unrest at that time, regarding the administration of public affairs, that we submit for Your Excellency's consideration the attached correspondence with the Speaker of the House of Commons. Perhaps Your Excellency will allow us to repeat what Lord Elgin said to the men of Glengarry, in reply to their address; "I recognize in it evidence of that vigorous understanding which enables men of the stock to which you belong, to prize, as they ought to be prized, the blessings of well-ordered freedom, and of that keen sense of

principle which prompts them to recoil from no sacrifice which duty enjoins."
The letter goes on to make further representations to His Excellen-cy, and attached to it is the correspondence which was subsequently transferred by His Excellency to the Prime Minister. I put a question to the Prime Minister with regard to this matter and was informed by him that he would later -make a declaration to the House on the subject.
This announcement by the Prime Minister has not come as yet. I might now read the correspondence which was attached to this letter sent to His Excellency the Governor General:
Windsor Hotel, Ottawa,
May 15 th, 1918.
Hon. E. N. Rhodes,
Speaker of the House of Commons.
Sir,-
The delegation of farmers from Ontario, Quebec and other provinces which held several conferences here yesterday charged us to transmit certain information to you with the respectful request that you will convey it to the House of Commons.
The conference yesterday afternoon composed of several thousand farmers decided unanimously to present itself at the House in the evening, with the request that two of its members he heard at the bar, in pursuance of the resolution duly adopted in the morning and forwarded to you. The Prime Minister, who was informed of this intention, referred us to the acting leader of the House, the Hon. Mr. Sifton. The request proffered while the delegation was in and about the precincts of Parliament was refused by the Hon. Mr. Sifton on behalf of the Government. The delegation therefore, in a most orderly manner, returned to its meeting place, where it unanimously endorsed the address which its representatives hal intended reading to the House, and directed us to forward it to you.
It is as follows:-
To the Honourable the Speaker,
and Members of the House of Commons, of Canada, in Parliament assembled.
Mr. Speaker and Gentlemen
of the House of Commons:-
On behalf of thousands of Ontario farmers assembled in this city to-day, we warmly thank the House for the proof it has given that it desires to keep in sympathetic touch with the citizens from whom it derives its dignity and authority. We believe we express the sentiments of all thoughtful citizens when we say that this departure in Canadian Parliamentary practice, following so closely upon the speech to this House and the Senate, of the President of the American Federation of Labour, is an agreeable recognition of the new relationships which the war is producing, as between those who govern and those who are governed by consent.
That portion of Canadian labour which is so vital to the prosecution of the war, and which we represent, appreciates' to the full the evidence of loyalty which the House of Commons gave in August, 1914, to the democracies of the Western Hemisphere in its instant support of the motherland in her hour of need. We
trust that the spontaneous action then taken will be justified by a continuation of those habits of freedom which it has long been the peculiar privilege of Canadians to maintain. These privileges are all the more appreciated in view of the long struggle for responsible government which was undertaken against the opposition of those who exercised arbitrary authority, and who feared the free expression of opinion, in the press and by the spoken word.
We are sure the House will permit us to say also, that the citizens generally have observed with gratitude that the House has shown a larger independence of thought and speech than has been customary under the system of partisan Government. We should fail in the duty of being candid which is cast upon us by the readiness of the House to hear us, if we did not express our concern regarding another tendency that has been observed in the House where the public will is believed to be supreme.
The increasing frankness of discussion so noticeable here, has been accompanied by a tendency to silence on the part of members of the Cabinet, who in reality, are, as one of four distinguished members has said "only a committee of this House."
The unrest in the country which has brought about the unexampled spectacle of thousands of farmers leaving the important work of planting their crops, to come to the capital to remonstrate with the Government, is known to every member of the House of Commons. We beg leave to intimate that this unrest is not related merely to the special matter which was discussed with the Premier and members of his cabinet to-day. We cannot disguise from the House an apprehension that the liberties, of which the popularly elected branch of the Legislature is the bulwark, may be dangerously curtailed during the period that the House is not sitting. In proof that this dread is not illusory, we would venture to inform the House that, in common with our fellow citizens, here and throughout the country, we have observed certain innovations, the continuation of which we believe would be fraught with serious results to the confidence which the subjects of His Majesty have hitherto reposed in the working of that responsible government for whose unimpaired preservation forty thousand Canadian soldiers have laid down their lives.
Will the House permit us to speak more plainly what is in our minds? We have never believed that the conditions produced by the war demanded flagrant departures from the honoured processes of law enjoined by the constitution while Parliament is in session or is near assembling. We believe that reliance upon Parliament, instead of upon arbitrary authority, most effectively honours the guarantees of freedom which axe embedded! in the constitution. One considerable departure from sound practice may be accepted, but repetitions of it may be exceedingly dangerous, especially under such circumstances as now beset the State.
We, therefore, beg leave to remind the House of several instances in which, it seems to us, the liberties of the people and of their repre-. sentatives have not been given sufficient consideration.	.
Twelve days before the meeting of Parliament in January, 1916, the authorized Canadian Army was doubled from 2'50,000 to 500,000 men. No British Army had ever been doubled without recourse to Parliament. That it was done in Canada caused students of British

history to enquire whether anything had oc-cured to warrant such a disregard of Parliament. Though this House of Commons has inherited some of the consequences of such an innovation, we desire to coniine our respectful remonstrances to more recent events.
During the session there were riots in the city of ^ Quebec. The House desired to discuss the serious situation thus created, and was entitled to declare what measures might be taken to prevent a renewal of such unhappy occurrences. It did not escape the notice of the country that immediately before the House proceeded to discharge its duty, there was put upon the table a completed law, in the form of an Order in Council, which arbitrarily took out of its control the very question which the House of Commons was about to discuss.
Later there were other departures from the traditional practice of British law by equally astonishing proceedings. An Order in Council was given to the House as a matter of information providing for the registration of the human power of the country, and setting up an entirely new criminal code in connection therewith, by creating several methods of punishment hitherto unknown to Canadian civilization. Surely such departure should not have been attempted in such a manner. Punishments created without the assent of Parliament naturally tend to provoke hostility. We feel we are performing a national duty in respectfully calling attention to such conditions.
The Order in council endorsed by Both Houses on April 18th virtually sweeps away the Military Service Act. The resentment It has created is known to this House, members of which are known to regret that the elements of the constitution were ignored in this proceeding; and that the method of presenting a practically executed decree, while withholding disclosure of the facts on which it may be based, cannot easily be justified to the constituents of a newly elected Parliament.	[DOT]
The curtailment of the liberty of written and spoken speech contained in the Order in Council given to the public on April 16 has especial concern to all who are aware of the history of free discussion in Canada and other parts of the British Empire. We are sure we need not beg the House to examine Its provisions in order to appreciate how a doctrine of the essential infallibility of the Government may be forced upon a free people on pain of a fine of five thousand dollars and five years' imprisonment. The House, to our extreme regret, has been faced with a notification of the intended curtailment of the privilege of a member of Parliament to declare his mind, and the right of his constituents to know what he has uttered. That this unique warning to a freely elected British assembly was halted for several weeks on the Order Paper, we venture respectfully to attribute to you, Mr. Speaker, as the appointed guardian of the liberties of the House and also of the people. It has been noted that the Prime Minister, in withdrawing the measure, viewed with so much apprehension from outside the House, announced that it is likely to be reintroduced next session.
Perhaps the House may not be offended to learn that cognizance has also been taken of a notice issued to it within the last week to the effect that It must curtail Its discussion of vital national affairs, and withdraw from its precincts within a few days, or be summoned hither during the hottest and most Inconvenient month of the year. That such a direction

should be issued without apparent recourse to fhe judgment of the House causes reflective citizens to wonder what has happened to the freedom Canadian institutions have hitherto enjoyed.
Mr Speaker, and gentlemen of the House of Commons, the disquiet of the country of which we are the humble and inadequate exponents and which demonstrates sadly the increasing dangers to our national unity, which, if we lose it, we shall have lost all indeed, cannot be allayed by a persistence in the courses we have so imperfectly sketched.
Will the House permit us, with much deference, but much earnestness to repeat the reminder of one of its members that the Government is a Committe of this House vested with the executive powers of Parliament. The responsibility of government, therefore, is ultimately upon this House. Nothing appears to have been done to make the position of members of Parliament, with regard to the carrying out of the war policy, correspond to the status which they enjoyed before the practice crept in of making them subservient to those whom they created and whom they might destroy.
In this prolonged crisis of the national fate the hour has arrived to re-establish the inherent freedom of the House of Commons. We are certain that in that restoration the people of Canada will sustain you, and that the sacrifices of war will ultimately be justified and honoured in the blessings and progress of peace.
May we inform you that we remain at the Windsor Hotel, where we shall be happy to receive whatever answer the House may return to this address.
We are, Mr. Speaker,
Yours very sincerely,
I beg to remind the Government, also, of the conclusions of the first report of the Select Standing iCommittee on Agriculture, which has just been adopted by the House. For three weeks the report of the committee lay on the table and no motion was made to have it concurred in by the House. The conclusions of that report are most important and read:
(a)	That actual farmers who have been called up shall be given leave of absence and
(b) That no actual farmers be required to report until all others in the class affected by the Order in Council of 20th April, 1918 have been put in service ; such leave of absence and delay In reporting to be conditional upon their actual employment In farming.
The other day, when the estimates of the Department of Agriculture were being discussed in committee, I inquired from the Minister of Agriculture what was the policy of the Government with regard to the exemption of farmers. The minister replied that I surely could not expect him to make a declaration of policy, but should put my question to the leader of the Government. I inquired from the Prime Minister as to the change of policy, if any, that was contemplated, and drew his attention to the fact that though the .Minister of Militia and Defence had told the House that the

boys on -the farm would not be called before the city boys and that instructions to that effect had been sent to the registrars for their guidance in- sending out notices, those instructions were not being followed. The Prime Minister told me he would bring the matter to the attention of the Minister of Militia and Defence. The boys on the farms are being called up as a matter of fact. Some time ago the Deputy Minister of Agriculture wired to Mr. J. J. Morrison, Secretary-Treasurer of the United Farmers of Ontario, Toronto, as follows:
Tour wire 18th to Minister re leave of absence lor farmers. Communicated with Mr. Stone-house, Agricultural representative Toronto, who replies officer commanding district states no leave being refused to farmers. Please see Stonehouse and furnish him with any specific cases you have. After seeing him, if still reason for complaint, kindly communicate with me.
Deputy Minister of Agriculture, Ottawa.
I wish to bring the attention of this House to one fact of which I am myself a witness. There is a conflict of authority between the representative of the Minister of Agriculture on the Leave of Absence Boards and the officers who compose these boards. The boards are composed of three or four officers who sit in a committee, and the representative of the Minister of Agriculture is there simply in an advisory capacity. I have seen oases in Quebec where I have myself acted as counsel for the farmers who were claiming exemption under the Leave of Absence regulation, and on three or four different occasions Hon. Mr. Garneau, the representative of the Minister of Agriculture on the Leave of Absence Board has recommended that leave of absence be granted, but leave was not granted. I am told by Mr. Morrison, the secretary of the United Farmers of Ontario, that yesterday Mr. Stonehouse, the representative of the Minister of Agriculture in Toronto, advised him that ha was powerless to obtain leave of absence for the farmers who were claiming it before the Leave of Absence Board. There is therefore a conflict of authority, igurely if the Government are in earnest when they state to this House and the country that the boys on the farm will not be called up until after the city boys have been called, means can be found of sending sufficiently plain instructions to the registrars [DOT] to that effect. I have talked this matter over with some of the officials of the Department of Militia and Defence, and they inform me that the whole thing is in the hands of the Minister of Justice, who has
charge of the administration of the law. Surely there should be some understanding between the Minister of Militia and Defence, the Minister of Agriculture, and the Minister of Justice, as to the instructions that shall be sent to the registrars and the steps which shall be taken to see'that such instructions are carried out.
I have been given leave by the right hon. leader of the Government to ask him a question, and this is the question I am going to put: Has the Government adopted any policy to provide for cases of extreme hardship and for cases in which production would surely be diminished? For instance, the case of the farmer's son who is the only one left to work the farm, or where the son is the sole support of incapacitated parents. I see by to-night's Star that an announcement on this question was supposed to be made to the House. I would ask the acting leader of the Government to make a plain statement on this matter, which is causing a great deal of unrest in the country.

subsubtopic: GENERAL, THE HOUSE OF COMMONS AND THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The Government has given and is still giving the most careful and earnest consideration possible to cases of extreme hardship that may occur in the working out of the Military Service Act and the Order in Council which has been passed more recently. These cases of hardship will be considered not only as they affect farmers but others as well. There will be no distinction made as to classes in which similar cases, or equal cases, of extreme hardship occur. In reference to those cases, an Order in Council has been considered and has been passed, and will be issued to the public, accompanied by regulations which are now receiving the consideration of the Government. These will be framed and published simultaneously with the gist or essence or full text of the Order in Council.

I do not know that my statement could go beyond the words which I have just now addressed to the House.

SECRET SESSION OF PARLIAMENT-ALLEGED DISCLOSURE OF PROCEEDINGS.
speechtext:
The very applause which has greeted the declaration of my right hon. friend (Sir George Foster) must show him that the Government has taken the proper action in doing what it has just done. The more liberal the execution of this new order is the better it will be. In connection with this matter I want to call the attention of the House to a question which is one that affects its privileges. I am glad to see the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) in his seat. Respecting the very subject that has just been dealt with, I find that the Evening Journal says:
Mr. J. a Armstrong, member for East Lambton, who was asked to resign, has issued a vigorous reply to the petitioners.
Mr. Armstrong throws Some new light on the secret session of Parliament and states that Mr. Lloyd George in an appeal to Canada asked for more men even if production suffered.
If it be true that the hon. member for East Lambton has given out a statement of what took place in the secret session, it is a breach of the privilege of Parliament. He had no right to do so. Nobody will dispute that. It was well understood that it was a secret session, and so far nothing has been said with regard to it. But if it be true that the hon. member for East Lambton has said what is here alleged, I repeat, it would be a breach of privilege. The paper further says:
Mr. Armstrong says in part:
In the secret session of Parliament held before deciding on the setting aside of exemptions, word was received direct from Lloyd George to send men and more men, even if production did suffer. This is only one of many urgent appeals received from the Government.
I think every man who heard the words spoken by the Prime Minister on that occasion-and he is the only man who spoke, -will agree with me when I say that I am sure the hon. member for East Lambton did not understand, or represent, what was said by the Prime Minister if he understood him to attribute to Lloyd George the words: "Even if production did suffer." There was not a word of that kind said, and I call upon the Government to take

such action as they think should be taken in regard to such a matter. I do not press for any answer to-day, but I .must protest and nobody will contradict my word, when I say that the hon. member for East Lambton had no right to repeat what was said in this House at a secret session.
